name: Threat Assessment
title: Threat Assessment
answer: Threat assessment is the process a trained school team uses when a student may pose a danger to others, gathering information, judging the level of concern, and deciding how to respond. AI has no place in the judgment itself, because these decisions shape a student's education, safety, and future and must be made by people. AI may only assist with documentation, using approved tools under a signed agreement.

sections.body: Threat assessment is how a school responds when a student may endanger others. A trained team collects information, weighs how serious the concern is, and chooses a response. What the team decides can change a student's schooling, safety, and life ahead, so every judgment has to come from people. AI can support the paperwork side, and only through tools the school has approved. The idea draws a firm line between machine help with records and human ownership of the decision.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a team member may use an approved tool, one covered by a signed agreement, to arrange notes or prepare a draft summary of how the team worked through its process. The text does not divide this guidance by grade band, so the same rule applies wherever a team operates. What the tool must never do is receive threat assessment information through a general chat tool, because these records are highly sensitive and can fall under strict legal rules. The team's own thinking, built from evidence and interviews, stays the source of the decision. The tool only helps put the team's process into words.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea's evidence as research. It states that research has shown people tend to go along with decisions a machine makes first, even poor ones (Krugel et al., 2023). Applied here, a tool that scores a student's risk could anchor a team's judgment in ways that harm the student. That is why the text says threat assessment teams should form their own views from evidence and interviews rather than from machine scores.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are strict. Threat assessment information must never be entered into a general chat tool, and any AI use in documentation must stay with approved tools under a signed agreement. The records are highly sensitive and may be subject to strict legal rules. The deeper risk is that a machine's first output can pull a team toward it, even when it is poor, so a risk score could distort the team's judgment and harm the student. The decisions themselves, about a student's education, safety, and future, remain with people, who base their views on evidence and interviews rather than machine scores.
